title: Test Your Understanding: How to Approach Any System Design Problem
description: Requirements, scope, estimates, high-level design, and trade-offs — the process, not the buzzwords.

questions.question: You're in a 45-minute interview and the prompt is "Design Instagram." What should you do in the first five minutes?

options.text: Draw Kafka, Cassandra, and S3 and explain how they connect
Ask clarifying questions about core features, users, scale, and latency expectations
Write the full SQL schema for photos, users, and follows
Calculate exact storage for 10 years of photos before any diagram

questions.explanation: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements first. Assumptions stated aloud let the interviewer steer. Schema and technology choices come after you know what you're building and for whom.

questions.question: A product manager asks for v1 of a URL shortener with shorten, redirect, and a full analytics dashboard with geo breakdowns. You're leading the design review. What's the best scope response?

options.text: Build everything in v1 because analytics was mentioned
Propose v1 as shorten + redirect; document analytics as v2 with an extension point for event logging
Remove redirect from v1 to ship analytics faster
Decline the project until all features are defined

questions.explanation: Scope control means an explicit MVP and non-goals. Core user value (shorten + redirect) ships first; analytics can follow once redirect traffic is validated. Extension points show foresight without over-building v1.

questions.question: In a system design interview, you should always spend the first 15 minutes on detailed back-of-the-envelope calculations before drawing any architecture.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Estimate when numbers would change the architecture — not by default before any diagram. Typical flow: clarify → scope → high-level design → rough math on the hot path → deep dives. Over-indexing on math early eats time needed for trade-offs.

questions.question: After clarifying requirements for a read-heavy news feed (1000:1 read:write), you sketch a high-level design. Which element is most appropriate at this stage?

options.text: Exact shard key formula and number of Cassandra nodes
Boxes for clients, load balancer, API, cache, primary DB, and optional async queue with labeled read path
Complete ER diagram with every index and foreign key
Detailed JWT claim structure and refresh token rotation policy

questions.explanation: High-level design shows major components and one happy-path data flow. Shard counts and index design are deep dives after the skeleton matches requirements. Auth details are usually out of scope unless the prompt centers on security.

questions.question: You're designing a home timeline for a social app. One user has 50 million followers. Which deep-dive framing best demonstrates senior trade-off thinking?

options.text: "We'll use a NoSQL database because it scales."
"Push fan-out breaks for celebrities; I'd use hybrid push for normal users and pull or precompute for high fan-out accounts, trading write amplification for read latency."
"We'll skip timelines and only support profile pages."
"Kafka fixes fan-out."

questions.explanation: Strong answers name the bottleneck (fan-out), compare options (push vs pull vs hybrid), pick one, and state the trade-off. Technology alone doesn't explain why the problem is hard or how you mitigate it.

questions.question: Which is primarily a non-functional requirement?

options.text: Users can create a short link from a long URL
Redirect p99 latency must stay under 100 ms globally
Admins can deactivate abusive links
API accepts a JSON body with destination URL

questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe what the system does (features, flows). Non-functional requirements describe how well — latency, availability, consistency, durability, security. p99 redirect latency drives CDN, caching, and region choices.

questions.question: Stating explicit "out of scope" items in a design doc is a sign of weak planning because it leaves features undesigned.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Out-of-scope and non-goals are contracts for v1. They prevent scope creep and show prioritization. Future considerations can be documented separately without committing to build them in the first release.

questions.question: You're 25 minutes into an interview. You have a scoped requirement list and a high-level diagram, but you've spent 18 minutes explaining OAuth2 flows. What's the best recovery?

options.text: Continue OAuth in depth since you've invested the time
Acknowledge auth is standard session/JWT at the edge, pivot to the core bottleneck (e.g., feed fan-out or storage), and offer one clear trade-off
Restart the entire session from requirements
Skip trade-offs and list as many technologies as possible in the remaining time

questions.explanation: Time management matters. Defer generic auth unless the prompt is security-focused; redirect effort to the constraint that breaks at scale. One well-argued trade-off on the core problem beats finishing a tangential deep dive.
